title: "Exercise 7 — Fitting a resource selection function"
subtitle: "Class 7 · Theme 5"
date-modified: last-modified
---



::: {.objectives}
**Goals.** Build used and available samples; fit an RSF and read the
coefficients as odds ratios; check that estimates stabilise as availability
grows; change the availability domain and watch the answer move; fit all six
buffalo two-stage; and map the predicted selection surface.

**Time:** ~55 minutes. **Packages:** `amt`, `terra`, `sf`, `dplyr`, `tidyr`.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(amt)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
```
:::


## Setup


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
clean <- read.csv("data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz") |>
  transmute(id = individual.local.identifier,
            t  = as.POSIXct(timestamp, tz = "UTC"),
            x  = location.long, y = location.lat) |>
  filter(!is.na(x), !is.na(y)) |>
  distinct(id, t, .keep_all = TRUE)

trk <- make_track(clean, x, y, t, id = id, crs = 4326) |>
  transform_coords(crs_to = 32736)

# Covariates, projected to match the track
elev <- rast("data/kruger_elevation.tif")
terr <- terrain(elev, v = c("slope", "TRI"), unit = "degrees")
names(terr) <- c("slope", "tri")
lc <- rast("data/kruger_landcover.tif")

covs <- project(c(elev, terr, lc), "EPSG:32736")
names(covs)
#> [1] "elevation" "slope"     "tri"       "trees"     "grassland" "shrubs"   
#> [7] "cropland"
```
:::


::: {.callout-warning}
## Project the covariates once, at the start

The track is in UTM 36S. `amt`'s `extract_covariates()` will **not** reproject
for you — hand it a raster in EPSG:4326 and every covariate comes back `NA`,
and `glm()` then fails with `no (non-missing) observations`. Project once,
here, and the rest of the exercise just works.
:::

## Task 1 — Used and available


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2026)

cilla <- trk |> filter(id == "Cilla")

rsf_dat <- cilla |>
  random_points(n = nrow(cilla) * 10) |>
  extract_covariates(covs)

table(rsf_dat$case_)
#> 
#> FALSE  TRUE 
#> 35280  3528
mean(is.na(rsf_dat$elevation))
#> [1] 0
```
:::


`random_points()` applied to a track draws available points inside that
animal's **MCP** — so this is a **third-order** analysis: where does Cilla go
*within* the range she has already chosen?

### Your turn

**1a.** Standardise the covariates and add the infinite weights.
**1b.** Why weight the available points so heavily?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
covars <- c("elevation", "slope", "tri", "trees", "grassland", "shrubs")

d <- rsf_dat |>
  filter(if_all(all_of(covars), \(z) !is.na(z))) |>
  mutate(across(all_of(covars), \(z) as.numeric(scale(z))),
         w = ifelse(case_, 1, 5000))

nrow(d)
#> [1] 38808
```
:::


The used–available design is really an **inhomogeneous Poisson point
process**, and logistic regression is a computational device for fitting it.
The equivalence is exact only in the limit of infinitely many, infinitely
down-weighted available points. Giving the available points a large weight
(here 5,000) makes the logistic coefficients converge to the correct
point-process coefficients.

Standardising makes the coefficients comparable across covariates measured in
different units — "per one standard deviation" — and improves the numerical
conditioning of the fit.
:::

## Task 2 — Fit and interpret


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit <- glm(case_ ~ elevation + slope + tri + trees + grassland + shrubs,
           data = d, family = binomial(), weights = w)

round(summary(fit)$coefficients, 4)
#>             Estimate Std. Error   z value Pr(>|z|)
#> (Intercept) -10.8483     0.0173 -628.3246   0.0000
#> elevation     0.1425     0.0210    6.7763   0.0000
#> slope         0.2920     0.0218   13.4035   0.0000
#> tri          -0.2102     0.0297   -7.0803   0.0000
#> trees        -0.0447     0.0511   -0.8751   0.3815
#> grassland    -0.4771     0.0896   -5.3264   0.0000
#> shrubs       -0.2962     0.0528   -5.6118   0.0000
```
:::


### Your turn

**2a.** Express each coefficient as an odds ratio with a confidence interval.
**2b.** Which covariate has the strongest effect, and in which direction?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
res <- data.frame(
  term = names(coef(fit)),
  beta = coef(fit),
  se   = summary(fit)$coefficients[, 2]
) |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  mutate(
    RSS   = round(exp(beta), 2),                       # relative selection strength
    lower = round(exp(beta - 1.96 * se), 2),
    upper = round(exp(beta + 1.96 * se), 2),
    beta  = round(beta, 3)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(beta)))

res
#>                term   beta         se  RSS lower upper
#> grassland grassland -0.477 0.08958078 0.62  0.52  0.74
#> shrubs       shrubs -0.296 0.05277846 0.74  0.67  0.82
#> slope         slope  0.292 0.02178613 1.34  1.28  1.40
#> tri             tri -0.210 0.02968249 0.81  0.76  0.86
#> elevation elevation  0.143 0.02103398 1.15  1.11  1.20
#> trees         trees -0.045 0.05109606 0.96  0.87  1.06
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
r <- res[order(res$beta), ]
plot(r$beta, seq_len(nrow(r)), pch = 16, col = "#1f6f78", cex = 1.3,
     xlim = range(c(r$beta - 1.96 * r$se, r$beta + 1.96 * r$se)),
     yaxt = "n", ylab = "", xlab = "Coefficient (log scale, per 1 SD)",
     main = "Cilla: third-order selection")
segments(r$beta - 1.96 * r$se, seq_len(nrow(r)),
         r$beta + 1.96 * r$se, seq_len(nrow(r)), col = "#1f6f78", lwd = 2)
axis(2, at = seq_len(nrow(r)), labels = r$term, las = 1, cex.axis = 0.8)
abline(v = 0, col = "firebrick", lty = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){fig-align='center' width=624}
:::
:::


Read the table as **relative selection strength**: `RSS = exp(beta)` is the
factor by which the relative probability of use multiplies for a one-standard-
deviation increase in that covariate, holding the others fixed.

An `RSS` of 1 means no selection; the confidence interval tells you whether
you can distinguish it from 1.

Note the **intercept is not interpretable**. It absorbs the arbitrary ratio of
available to used points — change `n` and the intercept moves, while the
slopes do not. That is precisely why only *relative* statements are licensed.
:::

## Task 3 — Does availability sample size matter?

The number of available points is your choice. The estimates should stop
moving once you have drawn enough.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
multipliers <- c(1, 5, 10, 25, 50)

stab <- lapply(multipliers, function(m) {
  dd <- cilla |>
    random_points(n = nrow(cilla) * m) |>
    extract_covariates(covs) |>
    filter(if_all(all_of(covars), \(z) !is.na(z))) |>
    mutate(across(all_of(covars), \(z) as.numeric(scale(z))),
           w = ifelse(case_, 1, 5000))
  f <- glm(case_ ~ elevation + slope + tri + trees + grassland + shrubs,
           data = dd, family = binomial(), weights = w)
  data.frame(mult = m,
             term = names(coef(f))[-1],
             beta = as.numeric(coef(f))[-1],
             se   = summary(f)$coefficients[-1, 2])
}) |> bind_rows()

stab |>
  select(mult, term, beta) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = mult, values_from = beta) |>
  mutate(across(-term, \(z) round(z, 3)))
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   term         `1`    `5`   `10`   `25`   `50`
#>   <chr>      <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 elevation  0.171  0.128  0.14   0.128  0.136
#> 2 slope      0.374  0.268  0.266  0.272  0.265
#> 3 tri       -0.24  -0.152 -0.176 -0.191 -0.187
#> 4 trees     -0.1   -0.045 -0.089 -0.088 -0.082
#> 5 grassland -0.613 -0.444 -0.536 -0.524 -0.535
#> 6 shrubs    -0.405 -0.273 -0.322 -0.316 -0.33
```
:::


### Your turn

**3a.** Have the coefficients stabilised?
**3b.** What happens to the standard errors?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

terms <- unique(stab$term)
cols <- hcl.colors(length(terms), "Dark 3")
plot(range(multipliers), range(stab$beta), type = "n", log = "x",
     xlab = "Available points (× n used)", ylab = "Coefficient",
     main = "Estimates stabilise")
for (i in seq_along(terms)) {
  z <- stab[stab$term == terms[i], ]
  lines(z$mult, z$beta, col = cols[i], lwd = 2, type = "b", pch = 16)
}
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
legend("bottomright", terms, col = cols, lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.6)

plot(range(multipliers), range(stab$se), type = "n", log = "xy",
     xlab = "Available points (× n used)", ylab = "Standard error",
     main = "SEs shrink without limit")
for (i in seq_along(terms)) {
  z <- stab[stab$term == terms[i], ]
  lines(z$mult, z$se, col = cols[i], lwd = 2, type = "b", pch = 16)
}
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-align='center' width=816}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```
:::


The **coefficients** settle down: past roughly 10× the used sample they barely
move, which is the check you should always run and report.

The **standard errors keep shrinking** as you add available points — and this
is the crucial asymmetry. Availability points carry information about the
*landscape*, not about the *animal*. Drawing more of them makes your estimate
of what was available more precise, so the SEs fall, but you have not observed
the animal any more closely.

That is why **p-values in used–available designs are close to meaningless**:
you choose the sample size, so you choose the p-value. Report effect sizes,
confidence intervals, consistency across individuals, and validation.
:::

## Task 4 — Change the availability domain

Same animal, same covariates, different definition of "available".


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Third order: within Cilla's own MCP (what we did above)
third <- d

# Second order: within the MCP of ALL six animals — the population's range
pop_mcp <- hr_mcp(trk, levels = 0.99)

second <- random_points(pop_mcp, n = nrow(cilla) * 10, presence = cilla) |>
  extract_covariates(covs) |>
  filter(if_all(all_of(covars), \(z) !is.na(z))) |>
  mutate(across(all_of(covars), \(z) as.numeric(scale(z))),
         w = ifelse(case_, 1, 5000))

# How different are the two domains?
c(cilla_mcp_km2 = round(hr_area(hr_mcp(cilla, levels = 0.99))$area / 1e6),
  population_mcp_km2 = round(hr_area(pop_mcp)$area / 1e6))
#>      cilla_mcp_km2 population_mcp_km2 
#>                309               2939

f3 <- glm(case_ ~ elevation + slope + tri + trees + grassland + shrubs,
          data = third, family = binomial(), weights = w)
f2 <- glm(case_ ~ elevation + slope + tri + trees + grassland + shrubs,
          data = second, family = binomial(), weights = w)

data.frame(
  term = names(coef(f3))[-1],
  third_order  = round(coef(f3)[-1], 3),
  second_order = round(coef(f2)[-1], 3)
)
#>                term third_order second_order
#> elevation elevation       0.143       -1.290
#> slope         slope       0.292        0.120
#> tri             tri      -0.210        0.336
#> trees         trees      -0.045        0.381
#> grassland grassland      -0.477        0.224
#> shrubs       shrubs      -0.296       -0.414
```
:::


### Your turn

**4a.** Do any coefficients change sign or magnitude substantially?
**4b.** Which analysis is "right"?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
cmp <- data.frame(term = names(coef(f3))[-1],
                  third = coef(f3)[-1], second = coef(f2)[-1])

plot(cmp$third, cmp$second, pch = 16, col = "#1f6f78", cex = 1.4,
     xlab = "Third order (within own MCP)",
     ylab = "Second order (within population range)",
     main = "The domain changes the answer")
abline(0, 1, col = "grey50", lty = 2)
abline(h = 0, v = 0, col = "firebrick", lty = 3)
text(cmp$third, cmp$second, cmp$term, pos = 3, cex = 0.65)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){fig-align='center' width=624}
:::
:::


Points off the dashed 1:1 line are covariates whose apparent importance
depends on the domain; points in the upper-left or lower-right quadrants have
**changed sign** between the two analyses.

**Neither is "right".** They answer different questions:

- *Second order* — given the whole area the population occupies, where does
  Cilla place her range?
- *Third order* — given the range she has already established, where within it
  does she go?

A covariate can drive the first decision and be irrelevant to the second, or
act in opposite directions at the two scales — an animal may settle in a
grass-rich part of the park and then, within it, seek out the scarce shade.

**The obligation on you** is to state the order and the availability domain
explicitly, in the abstract, not buried in the methods. A habitat-selection
result without that information cannot be interpreted.

::: {.callout-important}
## This also resolves an apparent contradiction with Class 5

In Class 5 we compared used points against points drawn from the convex hull
of **all six animals** and found buffalo used grassland about 1.6× more than
it was available — apparent **selection**.

Here, within **Cilla's own MCP**, the grassland coefficient is *negative*.

Both are correct, and together they tell a coherent story: buffalo place their
ranges in the grassy parts of the landscape (a second-order preference), and
then, within a range that is already overwhelmingly grassland, they move
towards the scarcer other things it contains.

The availability domain for Cilla is 309 km²; for the population it is
2,939 km² — nearly ten times larger, and a very different menu. Reporting the
third-order coefficient as "buffalo avoid grassland" would be a serious
misreading.
:::
:::

## Task 5 — All six animals, two-stage


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit_one <- function(animal) {
  a <- trk |> filter(id == animal)
  dd <- a |>
    random_points(n = nrow(a) * 10) |>
    extract_covariates(covs) |>
    filter(if_all(all_of(covars), \(z) !is.na(z))) |>
    mutate(across(all_of(covars), \(z) as.numeric(scale(z))),
           w = ifelse(case_, 1, 5000))
  f <- glm(case_ ~ elevation + slope + tri + trees + grassland + shrubs,
           data = dd, family = binomial(), weights = w)
  data.frame(id = animal, term = names(coef(f))[-1], beta = as.numeric(coef(f))[-1])
}

ids <- unique(trk$id)
per_animal <- lapply(ids, fit_one) |> bind_rows()

per_animal |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = id, values_from = beta) |>
  mutate(across(-term, \(z) round(z, 2)))
#> # A tibble: 6 × 7
#>   term      Queen  Gabs Cilla Mvubu  Toni Pepper
#>   <chr>     <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 elevation -0.79  0.14  0.13  0.34 -0.01  -0.28
#> 2 slope     -0.11  0.2   0.28  0.44 -0.44   0.06
#> 3 tri        0    -0.29 -0.2  -0.44 -1.41  -0.03
#> 4 trees     -0.23 -0.37 -0.08 -0.34  0.05   0.35
#> 5 grassland -0.35 -0.99 -0.55 -1.05  0.18  -0.48
#> 6 shrubs    -0.64 -0.42 -0.35 -0.36  0.56  -1.02
```
:::


### Your turn

**5a.** Summarise across individuals: mean coefficient, SE, and a t-test against zero.
**5b.** Are the animals consistent?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pop_level <- per_animal |>
  group_by(term) |>
  summarise(
    mean_beta = mean(beta),
    se        = sd(beta) / sqrt(n()),
    t         = mean_beta / se,
    p         = 2 * pt(-abs(t), df = n() - 1),
    n_positive = sum(beta > 0),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(across(c(mean_beta, se, t), \(z) round(z, 3)), p = round(p, 4)) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(mean_beta)))

pop_level
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   term      mean_beta    se      t      p n_positive
#>   <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>      <int>
#> 1 grassland    -0.541 0.184 -2.94  0.0322          1
#> 2 tri          -0.394 0.213 -1.85  0.123           0
#> 3 shrubs       -0.37  0.213 -1.73  0.143           1
#> 4 trees        -0.103 0.112 -0.919 0.400           2
#> 5 elevation    -0.077 0.166 -0.466 0.661           3
#> 6 slope         0.072 0.127  0.568 0.594           4
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
boxplot(beta ~ term, data = per_animal, col = "#1f6f78", border = "grey30",
        las = 2, xlab = "", ylab = "Coefficient (per 1 SD)",
        main = "Individual coefficients, 6 buffalo")
abline(h = 0, col = "firebrick", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
stripchart(beta ~ term, data = per_animal, vertical = TRUE, add = TRUE,
           pch = 16, col = adjustcolor("black", 0.6), cex = 0.8)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){fig-align='center' width=672}
:::
:::


This is the **two-stage** approach: each animal is one observation, so the
degrees of freedom reflect the number of *animals* (6), not the number of
*points* (hundreds of thousands). That is the honest accounting, and it is why
the p-values here are far less impressive than those in Task 2 — as they
should be.

The `n_positive` column is worth as much as the p-value: a covariate with the
same sign in 6 of 6 animals is a consistent effect even if the mean is
imprecise, while one that is positive in 3 and negative in 3 is not a
population-level effect however tight the pooled interval looks.

With more animals you would move to a **mixed model with random slopes**
(Muff et al. 2020). A random intercept alone is not enough — it lets
individuals differ in overall intensity of use but forces them to share one
selection coefficient, which badly under-states the uncertainty.
:::

## Task 6 — Map the prediction


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Rebuild the covariate stack standardised the same way as the fitting data
cilla_mcp <- hr_isopleths(hr_mcp(cilla, levels = 0.99))
covs_crop <- crop(covs, vect(cilla_mcp)) |> mask(vect(cilla_mcp))

mu <- sapply(covars, \(v) mean(values(covs_crop[[v]]), na.rm = TRUE))
sdv <- sapply(covars, \(v) sd(values(covs_crop[[v]]), na.rm = TRUE))

z <- rast(covs_crop[[covars]])
for (v in covars) z[[v]] <- (covs_crop[[v]] - mu[v]) / sdv[v]

b <- coef(fit)
lin <- b[["elevation"]] * z[["elevation"]] +
       b[["slope"]]     * z[["slope"]] +
       b[["tri"]]       * z[["tri"]] +
       b[["trees"]]     * z[["trees"]] +
       b[["grassland"]] * z[["grassland"]] +
       b[["shrubs"]]    * z[["shrubs"]]

rsf_map <- exp(lin)
names(rsf_map) <- "rsf"

plot(rsf_map, col = hcl.colors(50, "Viridis"),
     main = "Predicted relative selection — Cilla")
points(cilla$x_, cilla$y_, pch = 16, cex = 0.15,
       col = adjustcolor("white", 0.4))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){fig-align='center' width=720}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why the legend has no units

The values are **relative**, proportional to the probability of use by an
unknown constant. A cell with value 4 is predicted to be used about twice as
intensively as a cell with value 2 — but neither is a probability.

It is standard practice to rescale the surface to 0–1, or to bin it into
ordered quantiles, purely for display. Do not let that rescaling tempt you into
calling it a probability of occurrence.

Note also that the map is only meaningful **inside the availability domain**.
Extrapolating an RSF beyond the range of covariate values the animal actually
encountered is unsupported — the model has no information there.
:::

## Self-check

::: {.quiz}
You double the number of available points and your p-values all become smaller.
What does this tell you about your covariates?

- [ ] They are more important than you thought
- [x] Nothing — you increased the precision of your description of availability, not of your observations of the animal
- [ ] The model is now overfitted
- [ ] The weights were wrong

::: {.quiz-feedback}
Available points are a description of the **landscape**, which you can sample
as finely as your computer allows. Drawing more of them sharpens your estimate
of what was on offer, so the standard errors fall — but you have not observed
the animal any more closely, and no new biological information has entered the
model.

This is why p-values are near-meaningless in used–available designs. What you
should report: effect sizes as `exp(beta)` on standardised covariates,
confidence intervals, consistency across individuals, and out-of-sample
validation.

It is also why the two-stage approach in Task 5 is so useful: it makes the
degrees of freedom reflect the number of *animals*, which is the sample size
you actually have.
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
In Class 5 you found grassland covers 56% of the broader availability domain
but 90% of used points, and concluded buffalo select grassland. A colleague
objects that grassland is the commonest habitat there. Is your conclusion
consistent?

- [x] Yes — used exceeds available, which is exactly what selection means
- [ ] No — you cannot select for the commonest habitat
- [ ] Only if the sample sizes are equal
- [ ] Cannot say without the p-value

::: {.quiz-feedback}
Selection is *use relative to availability*, so a habitat can be both common
and selected. 90% use against 56% availability is a ratio of about 1.6 — real
selection, and it matches the used/available table you computed in Class 5.

The common confusion runs the other way: an animal found mostly in the
dominant habitat is often described as "preferring" it when the use/availability
ratio is 1 or below. That is why raw use frequencies are never enough, and why
the availability sample is not optional.
:::
:::

## Before Class 8

- Avgar et al. (2016) on integrated step selection analysis.
- Re-read section 3 of Fieberg et al. (2021) — the interpretation section.
